newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court rules withholding tax constitutional.
newsitem.headline: German court rules withholding tax constitutional.

text.p: Imposing withholding tax on interest income does not violate Germany's constitution, the country's finance court decided on Wednesday.
The court said that a law passed in 1992 which changed the way interest income is taxed in 1993 was constitutional, thereby overruling an earlier decision by a Munich court.
Joerg Weigell, a Munich tax lawyer, had brought a case against the 1992 law, arguing it failed to fight the common strategy of seeking to evade withholding tax by shifting investments abroad.

Weigell, who could not be reached for comment, is entitled to appeal to Germany's constitutional court. But he must first wait for the finance court to publish the grounds upon which it made its decision.
The ruling is not related to plans by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government to reform the German tax system by cutting a net 30 billion marks in income and company taxes in 1998 and 1999.
